claims.text: An active-learning machine-learning interatomic-potential framework can obtain fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties for both solid and liquid high-entropy-alloy phases.
The proposed framework can reproduce solid and liquid phase free energies and derived thermodynamic properties within approximately 2% of explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed framework will reduce computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed framework will be three to five times faster than TOR-TILD for similarly complex systems.
Near melting, the relevant ordered or disordered solids and liquids exhibit significant vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions.
The intervention trains a machine-learning interatomic potential from selectively sampled high-fidelity ab initio data.
Uncertainty quantification will trigger targeted free-energy perturbation calculations in regions requiring refinement.
Selective sampling and targeted corrections will capture the relevant thermodynamic contributions while minimizing expensive molecular-dynamics sampling.
The method is applicable from elemental and binary systems through quinary or higher high-entropy alloys.
The method is applicable near fusion temperatures where anharmonic effects are non-negligible.
Moment tensor potentials offer a useful balance between accuracy and computational cost for multicomponent refractory high-entropy alloys.
Coupling a machine-learning potential to uncertainty quantification can adaptively refine the potential in high-error regions.
Sparse ab initio corrections in high-uncertainty regions will capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration interactions.
Targeted correction will preserve the fidelity of the free-energy landscape across solid and liquid phases while lowering computational demand.
Melting temperatures and entropy differences will agree with full ab initio molecular-dynamics results to within approximately 2%.
High compositional disorder in extremely complex multicomponent systems may degrade machine-learning-potential accuracy and alter the expected speed or error margins.
